feed.title: Wits AHEAD · Daily briefing
feed.subtitle: News, research, video and readings on AI, data and human capability in higher education, curated every morning.
feed.rights: Wits AHEAD Research Group, Wits School of Education, University of the Witwatersrand

entry.title: South African ICT skills survey finds AI skills demand outpacing university and TVET pipelines
entry.summary:
The 2026 IITPSA ICT Skills Survey, run by the Institute of Information Technology Professionals South Africa with Africa Analysis and released on 30 October 2026, finds that demand for artificial intelligence skills, among AI engineers, machine learning engineers, generative AI specialists, prompt engineers and AI governance officers, is rising faster than South Africa's university and TVET pipelines can supply. About 80 per cent of ICT practitioners surveyed said AI had already reduced their workload or task complexity, while respondents named a lack of workplace experience, education and training gaps, limited diversity and the emigration of experienced professionals as the main causes of the skills shortage.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Wits AHEAD's fourth pillar is AI, graduate capability and employability; the survey's call for workplace-based learning and stronger industry-education partnerships speaks directly to the gap between what universities teach and what South Africa's AI economy now needs.

ITWeb (IITPSA and Africa Analysis) · Industry workforce survey (IITPSA and Africa Analysis)

entry.title: Study of five African countries finds AI adoption in universities outpacing curriculum and policy change

category.term: Ghana, Rwanda, Namibia, Kenya and Zambia

entry.summary:
A study by Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology's RetAIn project, published in Frontiers in Education and reported by the Ghana News Agency on 23 October 2026, surveyed 156 people and held focus groups with 77 stakeholders across Ghana, Rwanda, Namibia, Kenya and Zambia. It found that universities have introduced AI tools faster than they have changed curricula, lecturer training or governance, and that about half of respondents named costs such as tuition, data and devices as a barrier, with women, students with disabilities, and rural, low-income and part-time students most at risk of being left behind.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Wits AHEAD's sixth pillar is responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy; the study's country findings, policy without implementation in Rwanda, a curriculum lag in Namibia, uncoordinated initiatives in Ghana, mirror the governance gaps Wits AHEAD tracks across the Global South.

Ghana News Agency, reporting a Frontiers in Education study by KNUST's RetAIn project · National news agency report on a peer-reviewed study

entry.title: Office for Students tells universities to bring back in-person exams to protect assessment from AI
entry.summary:
England's Office for Students has told universities to consider returning to in-person, closed-book exams, vivas and practical tasks to keep assessment valid as artificial intelligence spreads. The guidance follows a four-month study with Advance HE, based on conversations with around 300 students and staff at more than 120 institutions, which found AI use is widespread and that some assessments are not fit for purpose. It is the first time the regulator has set out the institutional AI practices that could trigger intervention, including a lower quality award.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Wits AHEAD's first pillar is generative AI in higher education, including assessment and integrity; a national regulator moving from guidance to enforceable consequences is a marker other systems, including South Africa's, are likely to watch.

Times Higher Education · Established higher education press

entry.title: Graduates' wellbeing and civic contribution should be tracked alongside pay, British Academy argues
entry.summary:
The British Academy says current measures of graduate success focus too narrowly on salary, and wants work-life balance, long-term health and civic engagement tracked as well. It points to a government survey finding 24% of graduates volunteer formally at least monthly, against 17% of non-graduates, and proposes linking higher education data with health and crime datasets to build a fuller picture.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Wits AHEAD's fourth pillar covers graduate capability and employability beyond the first job; a national academy's push for broader outcome measures speaks directly to how the group frames "success" for its own candidates.

British Academy, reported by Times Higher Education · National academy report

entry.title: South Africa ranks second in Africa on new Commonwealth youth AI readiness index, behind Mauritius
entry.summary:
The 2026 Commonwealth Youth AI Readiness Index, compiled by the Ayre Think Tank from 1,128 sources across all 56 Commonwealth countries, places South Africa 13th overall with 56.8 out of 100, second in Africa behind Mauritius (64.4, eighth globally). The index projects AI could add between US$4.7 billion and US$13.7 billion to South Africa's economy over ten years, depending on the scenario.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Wits AHEAD's sixth pillar is responsible AI, equity and policy; national readiness indices like this shape the policy case for investment in AI skills and governance across the Global South.

University World News (from African Insider) · Established higher education press

entry.title: Youth unemployment eases slightly to 47.3% as overall unemployment rises to 33.7% in the third quarter of 2026
entry.summary:
The official unemployment rate rose by 0.1 of a percentage point to 33.7% in Q3 2026, as employment grew by 101,000 to 16.8 million but the labour force grew faster still. Youth unemployment (15 to 34) eased by 0.1 of a percentage point to 47.3%: unemployed youth fell by 23,000 to 5.0 million, while employed youth fell by 5,000 to 5.5 million.

Why it matters for AHEAD: This is the figure the group uses for graduate pathways and just transitions. Pillar 4 asks whether AI is narrowing or widening this gap for exactly this cohort.

Statistics South Africa · National statistics office

entry.title: University AI policies focus on cheating but leave data risks largely unaddressed, commentary warns
entry.summary:
A commentary in University World News argues that universities have written detailed rules against AI-assisted cheating while leaving far less guidance on how staff and researchers may put institutional, student or research data into AI tools. It cites a UK survey in which 63% of 49 higher education institutions had adopted some AI tool, yet only 37% had examined risks beyond their immediate supplier, and points to a University of Osaka leak affecting 77,851 people as a reminder that the bigger risk is often a conventional data failure, not the AI model itself.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Pillar 6, on responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, this is a prompt to check that university AI governance, including the group's own, covers data handling and not academic integrity alone.

University World News · Established higher education press (commentary)

entry.title: Wits opens a Global Higher Education Futures Centre, with a dedicated generative AI pedagogy hub
entry.summary:
The University of the Witwatersrand has formally opened its Global Higher Education Futures Centre, convened at an inaugural webinar on 30 September that drew more than 170 educators, institutional leaders and policymakers. The centre is organised around nine hubs, including one dedicated to generative AI pedagogy, and is framed as a response to what its founders call a polycrisis of climate breakdown, geopolitical tension, generative AI disruption and inequality in the Global South. Its founder, Professor Ruksana Osman, and director, Dr Bernadette Johnson, say the centre will centre Global South knowledge production rather than import ready-made models from the north.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, a South African university is building its own framework for thinking about AI's disruption of higher education, rather than adopting one designed elsewhere, which is exactly the Global South-led, equity-centred approach Wits AHEAD exists to support.

University of the Witwatersrand · University announcement

entry.title: Wording of university generative AI policies shapes how students and teachers actually behave, study finds
entry.summary:
Researchers analysed generative AI policies from 101 United States universities and interviewed 20 students and 20 faculty members about how the rules are actually followed. They found that the exact wording of a rule, not just its substance, changes how students behave: a rule framed around dishonesty made students hide their AI use out of fear, while a rule framed around accountability encouraged them to be transparent about it. Teachers, meanwhile, said they had taken on extra approval work and had no reliable way to check whether students were complying.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, the study is a reminder that a generative AI policy is only as good as its wording: universities writing or revising their own rules on AI in teaching and assessment need to test not just what a rule permits, but how students and staff will read and act on the words themselves.

arXiv preprint (University of Maryland and University of Iowa researchers) · Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed)

entry.title: How deeply students engage with an AI chat, not how often they use it, predicts better coursework, large Australian study finds
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Queensland and Monash University studied 1,681 students across 40 university courses who used AI companions built into resource creation, peer moderation and practice tasks. Coding 829 conversation threads for cognitive engagement and modelling nearly 3,000 task sequences, they found that students who engaged more deeply with the AI, rather than simply chatting with it more often, produced higher-quality final work regardless of how many messages they exchanged. After an incorrect attempt, students who talked to the AI made fewer further attempts but were more often right when they tried again.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 2, the finding matters for any institution building analytics around AI tool use: counting how often students open a chatbot tells you little about learning, so systems meant to support student success need to look at the depth of engagement, not the frequency of clicks.

University of Queensland and Monash University (arXiv preprint, submitted to the Journal of Computer Assisted Learning) · Working paper (arXiv preprint, submitted to the Journal of Computer Assisted Learning)

entry.title: Grade the process, not just the AI-era output, Bristol pro vice-chancellor tells student success conference
entry.summary:
Speaking at Times Higher Education's Student Success UK and Ireland conference, Tansy Jessop, pro vice-chancellor for education and students at the University of Bristol, said universities have moved past simply policing acceptable use of generative AI and should instead design assessments that reveal how a student reached their answer. She described a Bristol computer science case in which robot-design submissions were often found to be purely AI-generated, prompting staff to instead hand students a finished robot and ask them to work out how it was built. Jessop said the approach should help students develop skills that AI cannot easily replace, including curiosity, critical thinking and collaboration.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, it offers a concrete, classroom-level answer to the assessment integrity question: rather than chasing unreliable AI detectors, build tasks that make a student's thinking visible and keep a human judge in the loop.

Times Higher Education · Established higher education press

entry.title: AI-generated 'slop' papers published under prominent academics' names without their consent
entry.summary:
A cluster of look-alike journals has published AI-generated papers under the names of prominent academics, including Stanford's Jure Leskovec and Fei-Fei Li, who say they never wrote or submitted the work. Times Higher Education reports that one paper reappeared under different author names within days of being flagged and removed, and that the journals share an editor-in-chief and board members who did not know they had been listed. The three journals, registered only in 2026, charge authors between ten and two hundred US dollars per paper.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, the episode shows how generative AI can be used to fabricate not just research findings but researchers' own identities, which is why responsible AI policy for higher education must extend to publishing integrity and not stop at the classroom.

Times Higher Education · Established higher education press

entry.title: Staff overestimate how much students use generative AI, Manchester study finds
entry.summary:
A study of one social science school at a UK university found that academic staff significantly overestimate how often students use generative AI for their studies. Based on questionnaires with 45 staff and 86 students at the University of Manchester, staff rated student AI use at 5.23 on a seven-point scale, well above students' own average of 3.11. Students were also more positive than staff about AI's benefits for productivity and learning, and said they used it mostly to find answers, draft written work and improve grammar.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, the mismatch between what staff assume and what students actually do shows why generative AI policy and teaching design need to be grounded in evidence from students themselves, not in staff perception, especially as universities across the Global South weigh similar assumptions.

Frontiers in Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Habit, not enjoyment, drives ChatGPT use among distance students at the University of South Africa, study of 294 finds
entry.summary:
A study of 294 students at the University of South Africa, Africa's largest distance education institution, tested why students adopt ChatGPT using the UTAUT2 model. Habit was the strongest predictor of both the intention to use ChatGPT and actual use, followed by facilitating conditions such as guidance and resources, while enjoyment and the views of peers made no significant difference. The model explained 69.2% of students' intention to use the tool and 37.9% of their actual use.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, the finding that habit and institutional support, not novelty, drive use suggests universities should shape students' everyday AI routines through guidance and course design, especially in distance learning across the Global South.

Frontiers in Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Africa and Europe seek their own path on AI in science, with shared computing and genomic data on the agenda
entry.summary:
At an African Union and European Union meeting on AI in science on 26 October, held online instead of in Addis Ababa as planned, European Commission official Maria Cristina Russo said the United States and China were moving very far ahead and that Europe and Africa needed their own approach. Speakers called for shared regional computing, a continental framework for genomic data and benefit sharing, and measurable targets for women, who make up about one-fifth of the global data and AI workforce. Recommendations will go to an AU-EU research and innovation ministerial meeting postponed to 2027, University World News reports.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, the meeting puts data sovereignty, fair access to computing and the mobility of talent at the centre of AI policy, questions that decide whether African universities shape AI in research or only use it.

University World News · Established higher education press

entry.title: UNESCO: university enrolment in the Arab States has nearly tripled to almost 15 million, yet youth unemployment stands at 26%
entry.summary:
A new UNESCO report, The state of higher education in the Arab States, finds that university enrolment in the region has nearly tripled in 25 years to almost 15 million students, although the enrolment rate, 37% in 2024, still trails the global average of 44%. Women now make up nearly half of the region's STEM graduates, against just over a third worldwide, yet youth unemployment stands at 26%, roughly twice the global average. Launched in Doha on 4 November, the report sets out ten recommendations and notes that more than 70% of Arab States now write digitalisation into their national higher education plans.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 5, this shows what regional higher education data can reveal: rapid growth in access means little unless systems track whether graduates find work, the same test South Africa and the wider Global South face.

UNESCO (IESALC and UNESCO Office Beirut) · Intergovernmental body report

entry.title: Deep Learning Indaba video: Vukosi Marivate on governing AI in Africa and what a degree is worth now
entry.summary:
In a 36-minute interview recorded at the Deep Learning Indaba 2026 at Pan-Atlantic University in Lagos, Professor Vukosi Marivate, co-founder of the Indaba, Masakhane NLP and Lelapa AI and one of 40 experts on the United Nations Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, explains what advising governments on AI involves and why governing AI in South Africa touches every ministry. He argues that sovereignty means agency rather than building everything locally, that AI did not break assessment but exposed it, and that Africa should move from brain drain to brain circulation.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 4, his questions about what a degree is worth in the age of AI, and whether Africa is training cheap AI labour for export, go to the heart of graduate capability and just transitions in the Global South.

Deep Learning Indaba (YouTube) · Africa's machine learning community, official video channel

entry.title: South Korea vows to prosecute students using AI glasses in exams
entry.summary:
South Korea's Ministry of Education says it will treat cheating on the national university entrance exam with AI-powered smart glasses as a criminal matter from next year, after three students were caught wearing the devices during essay exams at Seoul universities. From 2027 those caught will face a three-year ban from the exam, up from one year, and inspectors will be posted at all 1,312 testing centres to watch for suspicious eyewear.

Why it matters for AHEAD: A stark marker of how fast generative AI tools are outpacing assessment integrity rules worldwide (pillar 1), and a reminder that detection and punishment are only part of the answer universities and systems will need.

Times Higher Education · Established press

entry.title: AI Article Reviews Dominate Human Peer Reviews at Their Best: Evidence and Policy Choices
entry.summary:
Gary King and Steven Worthington of Harvard's Institute for Quantitative Social Science compared AI-written peer reviews against 134 human reviews of 124 manuscripts collected between 2019 and 2026. They report that reviews generated by Claude Opus 4.8 outperformed the human reviews on every measure they constructed, were judged more accurate by the authors' own checks, and were preferred by three former journal editors in the large majority of head-to-head comparisons.

Why it matters for AHEAD: A sober, data-led challenge to how generative AI is used in academic practice, not only in the classroom (pillar 1): if AI can review research well, universities and journals need policy on when and how to use it, not simply whether to ban it.

Institute for Quantitative Social Science, Harvard University · University working paper

entry.title: Proposal 14: Student outcomes indicators
entry.summary:
England's higher education regulator, the Office for Students, has proposed replacing its single pass/fail graduate progression threshold with a basket of three benchmarked indicators for its Teaching Excellence Framework: continued progression into work or study, graduates' earnings against national benchmarks, and whether graduates report using what they learned, drawn from the Graduate Outcomes survey. The benchmarks would be adjusted for subject, geography, entry qualifications and students' socioeconomic background, rather than applying one fixed national threshold to every course.

Why it matters for AHEAD: This is a live test of pillar 5's central question: whether a data system built from several benchmarked indicators, rather than one blunt national threshold, can fairly judge and improve higher education outcomes.

Office for Students (OfS) · National regulator consultation

entry.title: UCT engineering pairs AI-enabled early warning with a multilingual support hub to lift student success
entry.summary:
Researchers in the University of Cape Town's Faculty of Engineering and the Built Environment describe a Student Success Project that combines an early risk-assessment framework, peer-led mentorship and a data-driven, AI-enabled support hub. The hub is paired with a multilingual digital glossary in isiXhosa, Sesotho, Kiswahili and Afrikaans, addressing language marginalisation alongside academic risk. The chapter appears in Constellations of Hope, a Club of Rome report on transformative learning.

Why it matters for AHEAD: A concrete, verified South African example of predictive analytics for student success (pillar 2) built around multilingual equity, showing that early warning data only helps students when the support that follows also speaks their language.

Globethics Publications (Club of Rome report) · Peer-reviewed book chapter

entry.title: AI literacy alone does not create graduate opportunity, Nigerian study of 450 students finds; technology readiness is what matters
entry.summary:
A survey of 450 Nigerian university students finds that both entrepreneurship education and AI literacy raise students' technology readiness, and that this readiness is what actually predicts whether they turn AI tools into real micro-entrepreneurial ventures. Perceived resource scarcity weakens graduates' entrepreneurial action directly, but strengthens the link between readiness and action once students do have the tools.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Direct evidence for pillar 4: access to AI alone does not create graduate opportunity in resource-constrained settings; it is capability-building and technology readiness that convert AI literacy into livelihoods.

Journal of Entrepreneurship in Emerging Economies · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Computational text indicators fail to improve, and can worsen, predictions of academic results, Salvadoran study warns
entry.summary:
Researchers at Universidad Salvadoreña Alberto Masferrer tested whether machine-learning-derived text indicators of students' epistemic norms could improve predictions of academic results beyond simple household and resource data. Across 263 students observed in two waves at five sites, the computational indicators added no reliable predictive value, and one version made predictions significantly worse after correcting for multiple comparisons.

Why it matters for AHEAD: A clear caution for pillar 5: AI-derived text or behavioural proxies should not be treated as fit for high-stakes education decisions without rigorous validation, a discipline Wits AHEAD applies to its own analytics work.

Journal of Applied Research in Higher Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: LMS activity, pacing and attendance are the strongest predictors of retention in blended courses, Turkish study finds
entry.summary:
A study in the Journal of Higher Education Policy and Management, by İrfan Ayhan of Kırşehir Ahi Evran University in Türkiye, examined how predictive analytics drawn from learning-management-system activity, pacing, assessment behaviour and attendance can flag students at risk in blended higher education courses. It finds these indicators are the strongest predictors of retention and argues that, used well, predictive analytics can strengthen early-warning systems and inform institutional strategy, provided institutions also attend to the ethics of using such data.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI and predictive analytics for student success, the study is a reminder that the data already sitting in most universities' learning-management systems, not just new AI tools, can power a workable early-warning system when combined with a clear ethical framework.

Journal of Higher Education Policy and Management · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Short hands-on workshop lifts science teachers' confidence in using AI for adaptive teaching, German pilot study finds
entry.summary:
A pilot study in the journal Frontiers in Education, by Mathea Brückner, Christoph Thyssen and Johannes Huwer of the universities of Konstanz, Education Thurgau and Education Freiburg, tested whether a short, hands-on workshop could raise lower secondary science teachers' confidence in using artificial intelligence for adaptive teaching. In a single-group pre-post design with 16 multiplier teachers in Germany, both the teachers' sense of AI's usefulness and their self-reported confidence in using it rose significantly after the workshop, with the two measures becoming strongly linked only afterwards. The authors caution that the small, self-reported sample shows change rather than proving the workshop caused lasting improvement.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, the study offers a concrete, low-cost format, a short hands-on workshop, that teacher-training programmes could test and adapt for building science teachers' confidence with AI tools.

Frontiers in Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: World Bank video: 'small AI', not big models alone, can widen opportunity in developing-economy education and jobs
entry.summary:
At the Global AI and Digital Summit in Seoul, recorded by the World Bank Group, President Ajay Banga opened a panel on how practical, locally adapted "small AI" tools, not only large general-purpose models, can expand opportunity in developing economies. Nigeria's Minister of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy Bosun Tijani joined Tridge chief executive Hoshik Shin and Amini founder Kate Kallot to discuss education, agriculture and public services, including a segment on lessons from using AI in education in El Salvador. The panel named reliable local data, affordable connectivity, computing power, skills and procurement systems as the conditions that let local innovators scale AI solutions.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on AI, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, the discussion grounds the promise of AI in the practical conditions, skills, infrastructure and procurement, that decide whether developing-economy universities and systems actually benefit, rather than only their better-resourced counterparts in the Global North.

World Bank Group (YouTube) · International financial institution, official video channel

entry.title: Review of generative AI ethics in higher education finds Africa only 11% of the evidence, calls for Ubuntu-informed governance
entry.summary:
A systematic review in Education Sciences, by Pearl Yarkor Yarboi and colleagues at the University of Ghana, examined 246 studies published between 2018 and 2025 on the ethics of generative AI in higher education, and found that African institutions account for only about 11.4 per cent of that literature, and Ghanaian institutions for just 2.8 per cent. It groups the recurring concerns into five domains, academic integrity, privacy and data security, transparency and accountability, equity and access, and AI literacy, and reports that Ghanaian institutions in particular show limited systematic governance.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's work on responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the review's call for contextualised, Ubuntu-informed ethical frameworks rather than imported Global North standards speaks directly to the group's own approach to generative AI in African higher education.

Education Sciences · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Systematic review of 50 studies finds university AI governance works best when oversight, integrity rules and data risk are managed together
entry.summary:
A systematic review in Frontiers in Education, led by Fritz D. Bacalso and colleagues at Cebu Technological University in the Philippines, screened 221 records against the PRISMA 2020 protocol and synthesised 50 studies on how higher education institutions govern generative AI. It finds that effective adoption depends on governance maturity: coherent oversight across university units, clear academic integrity and disclosure standards, and risk-based data governance, alongside efficiency and learning gains where pedagogical support accompanies the technology. The review also reports stark regional gaps, citing one study in which six South African universities had formal AI policies while none of the sampled institutions in Ghana or Nigeria had a publicly accessible governance framework.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's work on generative AI in teaching, assessment and integrity, the review's evidence that governance maturity, not access to tools alone, decides outcomes supports the case for African universities to build coherent, integrated oversight rather than policy that exists only on paper.

Frontiers in Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Systematic review proposes a two-part framework for generative AI and academic integrity in higher education
entry.summary:
A systematic literature review in the journal AI and Ethics, by Batool Hendal and Gobinda Chowdhury, analysed 274 coded findings from existing research on generative AI in higher education and grouped them into six themes, including its benefits and risks, the unreliability of AI-text detectors, and institutional policy and governance. From this evidence the authors propose an Academic GenAI Adaptation Framework built on two pillars, governance and infrastructure on one side and education and literacy on the other, as a practical route to adopting generative AI responsibly rather than simply policing it.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's work on generative AI in teaching, assessment and integrity, the framework offers African universities a structured alternative to detection-based policing, built from the accumulated evidence rather than a single institution's experience.

AI and Ethics · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Mixed-methods study of 1,685 publications and 48 interviews finds generative AI is reshaping assessment, not just fuelling misconduct
entry.summary:
A mixed-methods study in the journal SN Social Sciences, by Florieza M. Mangubat and Fernando N. Mangubat, combines a bibliometric analysis of 1,685 Scopus-indexed publications on academic integrity and assessment with interviews of 48 students and instructors at higher education institutions in the Cebu region of the Philippines. It finds that scholarly attention to the topic rose sharply after 2022, that students use generative AI for learning and academic tasks while remaining unsure what use is acceptable, and that instructors are responding by redesigning assessment toward process-oriented, authentic tasks rather than relying on AI-detection tools alone.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's work on generative AI in teaching, assessment and integrity, the finding that institutions in another part of the Global South are moving from policing to redesigning assessment echoes what African universities are already weighing, and strengthens the case for assessment reform over detection as the more durable response.

SN Social Sciences · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Systematic review of 463 studies finds AI in Global South universities still mostly administrative, not pedagogical
entry.summary:
A systematic review and bibliometric analysis in the journal Frontiers in Education, by Nomfundo Gladys Khoza and Freda van der Walt of the Central University of Technology, Free State, screened 947 records and included 463 peer-reviewed studies published between 2019 and 2025 on AI-enhanced pedagogies in higher education across the Global South. It finds that most AI applications still aim at technical efficiency and administrative functions, that genuine pedagogical integration remains limited, and that inadequate infrastructure, unequal access to digital tools, limited faculty readiness and ethical concerns are the main barriers, while locally adapted solutions and collaborative innovation stand out as the clearest opportunities.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's work on generative AI in teaching and on responsible, equitable AI policy, the review's finding that administrative use still outpaces genuine teaching innovation across the Global South is a reminder that African universities, including Wits, need deliberate investment in faculty readiness and locally adapted pedagogy, not just access to AI tools.

Frontiers in Education · Peer-reviewed journal article (systematic review)

entry.title: US universities race to launch AI majors as the count passes 100, nearly double in a year
entry.summary:
More than 100 United States universities now offer an undergraduate major in artificial intelligence within computer science departments, nearly double the number a year earlier, according to a database kept by Northeastern University's Center for Inclusive Computing. Bentley University's AI major has grown from a handful of students at its 2024 launch to nearly 100 this year, while MIT's AI and Decision Making major, started in 2022, is now the university's second most popular with 354 students enrolled. Administrators link the rush partly to student anxiety about an AI-reshaped job market and partly to employer demand for AI-skilled graduates; a May study found just over a third of 66 surveyed institutions offering an AI major require an ethics course.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's work on AI, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, the scale and pace of this shift in the Global North, and the patchy requirement for ethics training alongside it, is a marker Wits AHEAD can use to weigh how African universities should shape comparable AI qualifications responsibly rather than reactively.

WBUR · Public radio news report

entry.title: Study combines AI-TPACK and Freire's critical pedagogy to rethink AI in African STEM curricula
entry.summary:
Two University of South Africa researchers set out a conceptual framework for bringing artificial intelligence into STEM curricula across Africa, combining the AI-TPACK model with Paulo Freire's critical pedagogy. Drawing on a narrative literature review rather than new fieldwork, the paper surveys tools such as intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms and automated assessment, and argues these could ease the strain in overcrowded, under-resourced classrooms. It recommends culturally relevant, ethically grounded strategies that address infrastructure gaps, teacher capacity and contextual diversity so that AI adoption does not widen existing inequities.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's work on AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, the paper offers a critical, Africa-rooted framework for weighing AI's promise in STEM teaching against the continent's real constraints of infrastructure and teacher capacity, a caution that should temper any push for rapid AI adoption.

Eurasia Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education (University of South Africa) · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Survey finds most Built Environment students use AI chatbots but African universities still lack formal AI policy
entry.summary:
A survey of Built Environment students presented at the FIG Congress 2026 in Cape Town found that 74 per cent already use AI chatbots for academic purposes and hold broadly positive views of their support for learning, yet report minimal institutional guidance on their use. The authors, writing from Namibia and Nigeria, note that only a handful of South African universities, including the University of the Witwatersrand, the University of Cape Town, the University of Pretoria and the University of Johannesburg, have developed AI guidelines since 2024, against nearly 70 per cent of United States universities with written AI policies. They set out a roadmap for African universities to build contextually appropriate AI governance frameworks.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's pillar on responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the finding that most African institutions still have no formal AI policy, even as students widely adopt AI chatbots, shows how far governance lags behind practice, and the paper's roadmap gives a starting point for closing that gap.

FIG Congress 2026 (International Federation of Surveyors), Cape Town · Conference paper (International Federation of Surveyors)

entry.title: WISE and Education Collaborative partner with five African universities on an AI adoption pilot
entry.summary:
WISE, the World Innovation Summit for Education, and Ashesi University's Education Collaborative have launched an AI adoption pilot with five African universities: Bells University of Technology in Nigeria, Botho University in Botswana, KCA University in Kenya, the University of Kigali in Rwanda and Université d'Abomey-Calavi in Benin. Running from October 2026 to June 2027, each university is trialling a project suited to its own priorities, from curriculum-aligned AI tutors and adaptive learning tools to early-warning systems and institutional governance frameworks. The pilot builds on a 2025 baseline study of 47 African universities, which found AI adoption fragmented and governance thin.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's work on responsible AI governance, this is a rare multi-country trial that tests AI tools and institutional policy together across five very different African universities, offering early comparative evidence of what responsible adoption looks like in practice.

africa.com (WISE and The Education Collaborative, Ashesi University) · International education initiative announcement

entry.title: Early success indicators at a South African university: a data-centric approach to student success
entry.summary:
Philokuhle Majozi and Kgadi Mathabathe of the University of Pretoria have proposed an “early success indicators” framework that maps data points and support interventions across the whole student lifecycle, from before registration through to final assessment. Drawing on interviews with academic success coaches, institutional leaders and data scientists, the framework favours a strengths-based, proactive model over deficit-oriented “at-risk” early-warning systems.

Why it matters for AHEAD: This gives Wits AHEAD's predictive-analytics pillar a South African, strengths-based alternative to conventional early-warning models, directly relevant to designing retention interventions that support rather than merely flag struggling students.

Journal of Student Affairs in Africa · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Cambridge-led OpRaise report: AI markers favour style over substance in university essays
entry.summary:
Researchers from the Universities of Cambridge, Manchester Metropolitan and Nottingham tested three leading AI models, singly and in combination, on 761 undergraduate psychology essays from three UK universities. The models agreed closely with each other but less with human examiners, consistently rewarding longer, more complex writing regardless of academic merit and compressing marks toward the middle of the scale.

Why it matters for AHEAD: As Wits AHEAD weighs AI's role in assessment, this is rigorous, multi-institution evidence that automated marking still favours style over substance, a caution against replacing human judgement in Global South universities with far larger classes and fewer markers.

University of Cambridge, Manchester Metropolitan University and the University of Nottingham (OpRaise project) · University research report

entry.title: World Bank video: Korea Partnership Facility forum explores AI for education and skills
entry.summary:
The World Bank Group's YouTube channel has published a short film on this year's Korea-World Bank Group Partnership Facility forum, where officials from Korea's Ministry of Economy and Finance, World Bank specialists and a KAIST professor discussed how artificial intelligence can strengthen learning and prepare people for the jobs of the future. The Facility funds AI and digital programmes for education and skills systems in developing countries.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Pillar 4, it shows that international financial institutions now treat AI skills training as central to graduate employability and just transitions, not an add-on.

World Bank Group (YouTube) · International financial institution, official video channel

entry.title: Study finds South African universities' AI policies strong on student rules, thin on privacy and staff duties
entry.summary:
A qualitative study of the generative AI guidelines published by South African public universities finds that only 46 per cent of institutions had an institution-wide policy at the time of the analysis. Where guidelines existed, they set out detailed rules on transparency and student accountability, but covered privacy, data governance and staff accountability only briefly and mostly as advice rather than binding rules.

Why it matters for AHEAD: It is squarely Pillar 6 evidence for Wits AHEAD: the authors call for harmonised, privacy by design AI guidance across the sector, which is exactly the responsible AI gap the group tracks.

Universal Access in the Information Society · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Smartphone AI tools help STEM teachers in low-resource African classrooms move beyond chalk and talk, study finds
entry.summary:
A Universiti Sains Malaysia-led case study worked with ten STEM teachers from Nigeria, Botswana, Ghana, Namibia and Sierra Leone in a hands-on workshop using AI speech-to-image tools, smartphone block coding and circuit simulation. The teachers said the tools made abstract science concepts easier to show, let learners without laptops build coding skills on a smartphone, and let them test circuits safely before touching scarce real equipment.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Pillar 3, it is good evidence that carefully chosen, low-cost AI tools, not expensive hardware, are what can move STEM teaching in under-resourced African classrooms from chalk and talk to real inquiry.

ECNU Review of Education · Peer-reviewed journal article
